final:
I checked all three review issues against the code: one is a real bug to fix, one is worth an optional test fix, and one is only partly right. The verdicts are in `verdicts.json`, and I made no code changes and posted no replies. I didn't run the tests; the conclusions come from reading the code.

| # | Category | Verdict | Fix it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Correctness: indefinite-length input (`0x80`) | Partly valid | Optional |
| 1 | Unused code | Valid | Yes |
| 2 | Test quality: key curve mismatch | Valid | Optional |

**Issue 1: two useless encoder calls.** `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:114-115` create two encoders, write `r` and `s` into them, then throw the results away. Lines 117-121 build the same encoders again inside `writeDerSeq`, so lines 114-115 should just be deleted.

**Issue 2: every test uses the same key curve.** `ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42` makes a single EC key pair on the Java default curve (P-256 on the local Java 17). The same key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so at least two of the three tests use a curve that doesn't match the algorithm. The tests still pass, but only because of how the conversion code behaves:
- When the signature values are longer than expected, `integerToBytes` (lines 151-156) cuts them short.
- The shortened values then convert back and forth consistently, so the equality check still succeeds even though data was lost.

The fix is to generate a key on the matching curve for each test (P-256, P-384, P-521). This weakens the tests but isn't a bug in the shipped code.

**Issue 0: indefinite-length input.** The reviewer is half right:
- **`readInteger`:** correct. A length of -1 reaches `new byte[-1]` (`ASN1Decoder.java:170`), which throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException` rather than the declared `IOException`.
- **`readSequence`:** overstated. It does return an empty list, but its only caller (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:129-131`) already rejects that with an `IOException`.

The input is always a DER-encoded signature, and DER doesn't allow indefinite length, so valid signatures never reach this code. The only effect is that malformed input fails with the wrong exception type. Having `readLength` throw an `IOException` for `0x80` would be a cheap hardening fix.
